input:
Start-up

It is essential, before start-up, to confirm that the relief valve installed is the valve that has been specified for the duty. The nameplate should be read and the stamped set pressure checked against the set pressure given on the equipment data sheet; if any mismatch is found, work must stop and the mismatch must be reported, and the valve must not be put into service until the matter has been fully resolved. It should also be confirmed that the inspection tag is in date and that no test report for the valve is outstanding. Any transport gag or shipping restraint that was fitted for transit must be removed, and it must be confirmed that the restraint is completely clear of the spring and stem before the system is pressurised. The discharge line should be walked from the valve outlet through to its termination so that it can be confirmed that the path is open along its whole length: no blind flange left in place, no closed valve in the discharge path that is not locked open, and no temporary cap or plug remaining at the outlet. The inlet isolation valve, where one is fitted, must be confirmed fully open and locked or sealed in the open position, and the same check applies to any outlet isolation valve. Drains and vents on the inlet and discharge lines should be checked closed, and any tell-tale drain between the valve and its discharge header should be confirmed open to a safe place so that leakage past the seat shows there first. The valve body, bonnet and flange joints should be inspected for damage, corrosion and loose bolting, and the lever or cap confirmed to be in its normal position. The system pressure should then be raised slowly and in stages, holding at each stage so that the flange joints and the bonnet joint can be checked for leakage. The inlet pressure gauge should be watched as the pressure rises and the reading compared with the reading expected for the start-up stage, and any reading that does not follow the pressurising source should be investigated. As the pressure approaches normal operating pressure, the valve should be listened at for simmer or leakage past the seat. Finally, the start-up should be recorded in the shift log, including the valve identification, the checks completed and any defect found, with the defect reported through the maintenance system before the system is left in service.

Normal operation

The relief valve must be kept in service and available at all times while the protected system is pressurised. The valve must never be gagged, the lever must never be wired down, the discharge must never be blocked, and the set screw must never be adjusted; set-pressure adjustment is workshop work carried out under a test procedure, and it is never an acceptable field correction for a valve that lifts early or leaks. The valve should be made part of the normal operator round. On each round, the valve and its joints should be looked at for signs of leakage, corrosion, mechanical damage and loose bolting. Listening should be carried out for discharge noise, simmer or chatter carried through the discharge line. The discharge line downstream of the valve should be felt with the back of the hand where access is safe: a line that is warm when the valve has not lifted is an indication of leakage past the seat. The inlet pressure gauge should be read on the round and the reading entered in the round log, so that a slow rise in operating pressure towards the set pressure becomes visible in the record before it develops into an alarm. The area around the valve should be kept clear so that the nameplate, the lever and the discharge outlet remain accessible and visible. The discharge termination must be kept unobstructed: no stored material should be placed against it, no scaffold tied to it, and no temporary equipment hung from the discharge line. Leakage past the seat, damage, corrosion or a missing or out-of-date inspection tag should be reported through the maintenance system on the round on which it is found. Where a block valve arrangement allows the relief valve to be isolated, the isolation state should be treated as a controlled condition: the operating relief path must be open whenever the system is pressurised, and any change of isolation state must be made under the site permit procedure and recorded in the shift log, together with the time of the change and the name of the operator making it.

Alarms

Two alarms are fitted for this valve, and no others. The high inlet pressure alarm sounds when the pressure in the protected system rises above its alarm setting. When this alarm sounds, the pressure reading should first be checked against the local inlet gauge so that it can be confirmed that the rise is real. The pressure should then be reduced at its source: the heat input or the feed to the system should be cut by the normal operating procedure for the equipment being protected, and the manual vent to a safe location should be opened if the pressure continues to rise. The shift supervisor should be informed and the system kept under observation. It should be expected that the relief valve will lift if the pressure reaches the set pressure; a lift on a confirmed pressure rise is simply the valve doing its duty and is not by itself a defect. Personnel should stay clear of the discharge termination while the valve is lifting or may lift. The discharge alarm sounds when flow through the discharge line shows that the relief valve has lifted. When this alarm sounds, the operator should go to the valve and confirm the lift from the discharge indication, and should then find the cause of the overpressure in the protected system and remove it by the normal operating procedure. The lift should be recorded in the shift log, together with the pressure reached and the cause found. The valve should be watched to make sure that it reseats as the pressure falls, and after it has reseated it should be checked for continued leakage past the seat by means of the tell-tale drain and by listening at the discharge line. A valve that does not reseat, or that continues to leak after reseating, should be reported through the maintenance system, and the system pressure should be kept under observation until the defect has been dealt with. It should also be noted that a valve that has lifted is reported for inspection at the next opportunity, even when it reseats cleanly.

Shutdown

The relief valve should be taken out of service only when the protected system is depressurised, or when an alternative relief path is in service and has been recorded. The system pressure should be reduced in a controlled manner by the normal shutdown procedure, venting to a safe location, and it should be confirmed on the inlet gauge that the pressure has fallen and is stable before any isolation is made. The inlet isolation valve should be closed, and then the outlet isolation valve where one is fitted, and both valves should be locked and tagged under the site isolation procedure. The inlet line and the valve body should be drained through the drain connection to a safe place, and the discharge side should be vented so that no trapped pressure remains between the isolation valves. A check for trapped pressure should always be made before any flange is broken: the joint should be slackened slowly and work stopped at the first sign of pressure or discharge. The isolation should be recorded in the shift log and on the isolation register, together with the state of each valve in the line-up. Where the relief valve is removed for bench testing or overhaul, blind flanges should be fitted to the open inlet and discharge connections, the removed valve should be tagged with its identification and set pressure, and the removal should be recorded so that the protected system is not returned to service without a relief valve in place or an approved alternative. On return from test, the valve should be refitted with new gaskets, the test certificate should be confirmed to match the nameplate set pressure, and the line-up should be restored by means of the start-up checks set out in this chapter before the system is pressurised again.
